## Summary: Bivariate Predictors of No-Record Persistence (`no_record.cat`)

**Overview**

This stage repeated the full Step 3 bivariate analysis a third time, using `no_record.cat` — persistence of having no Minnesota employment record, isolated from employment instability — as the outcome. Combined with the blended and non-sustained-only analyses, this completes a full three-way decomposition across all sixteen variables. The results are the clearest yet: most variables that weakened when isolated to non-sustained employment come back at or above their original blended strength here, confirming that record-absence — not employment instability — is the dominant mechanism behind most of the disparities identified in this project.

**Variables confirmed as no-record-driven (majority or entirety of their blended effect lives here)**

| Variable | Blended | Non-sustained | No-record | Share attributable to no-record |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| English learner | V=0.096 | V=0.063 | **V=0.107** | Nearly all |
| Non-English home | V=0.072 | V=0.061 | **V=0.102** | Nearly all |
| took.ACT | V=0.078 | V=0.047 | **V=0.096** | Majority |
| ACTCompositeScore.filled | η²≈1.4% | ns | **η²≈1.91%** | Essentially all |
| attended.ps | V=0.182 | V=0.088 | **V=0.124** | \~Two-thirds |
| cte.achievement | V=0.098 | V=0.041 | **V=0.084** | Majority |
| sat.taken | V=0.043 | ns | **V=0.050** | Essentially all |
| total.cte.courses.taken | η²≈2.2% | η²≈0.17% | **η²≈1.54%** | Majority |
| RaceEthnicity (AI specifically) | 21.2-pt gap | 2.3-pt gap | 14.6-pt gap | \~Two-thirds |
| edr | V=0.021 | ns | V=0.034 | Essentially all |

This is the largest cluster by far — ten of sixteen variables. Every one of these was flagged in the non-sustained table as weakening dramatically; every one of them is confirmed here as recovering most or all of that strength.

**Variables confirmed as non-sustained-driven (mechanism runs the other way)**

| Variable        | Blended  | Non-sustained | No-record                    |
|-----------------|----------|---------------|------------------------------|
| Gender          | V=0.074  | **V=0.091**   | V=0.016 (barely significant) |
| Economic status | V=0.070  | **V=0.081**   | V=0.033                      |
| MCA.M           | η²≈0.2%  | **η²≈0.25%**  | ns                           |
| MCA.R           | η²≈0.07% | **η²≈0.14%**  | ns                           |

Four variables, all confirmed in this table as showing negligible-to-null relationships with record-absence specifically. Gender is the cleanest example in the entire project — its blended and non-sustained relationships are real, but its no-record relationship is barely distinguishable from noise.

**Variables genuinely mixed between both mechanisms**

| Variable | Non-sustained | No-record | Note |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| SpecialEdStatus | V=0.076 | V=0.067 | Splits nearly evenly |
| RaceEthnicity (Black specifically) | 7.8-pt gap | 5.0-pt gap | Splits roughly evenly |
| MCA.S | η²≈0.37% | η²≈0.14% | Only academic variable significant in both |
| pseo.participant | V=0.042 (complex shape) | V=0.043 (cleaner, protective shape) | Both real, different shapes |
| ap.exam | V=0.030 | V=0.041 | Weak in both, non-monotonic |
| Dem_Desc | V=0.019 | V=0.026 | Weak in both |

**Variables with no meaningful relationship to either mechanism**

`avg.unemp.rate` and `avg.wages.pct.state` were weakly significant only in the blended table and non-significant in both the non-sustained and no-record tables — the honest conclusion, reached only after running all three tables, is that their original blended significance was very likely a large-sample artifact rather than a real, attributable relationship with either mechanism.

**The central finding of this entire three-way comparison**

Disconnection in this population resolves cleanly into two distinct phenomena, and the vast majority of individual characteristics examined here belong predominantly to one or the other:

1.  **A "record-absence" cluster** (the larger group): postsecondary/academic exposure variables (attended.ps, took.ACT, ACTCompositeScore, CTE achievement and course count, SAT-taking), English learner and non-English-home status, American Indian identity, and regional geography (edr) all relate mainly to whether someone shows up in Minnesota's employment system at all.

2.  **A "genuine instability" cluster** (smaller but clear): Gender, Economic status, and MCA Math/Reading scores relate specifically to employment instability itself, largely independent of record-presence.

3.  **A genuinely mixed group**: SpecialEdStatus, Black identity specifically (distinct from American Indian), MCA Science, and PSEO participation don't sort cleanly into either camp — each shows a real, roughly comparable relationship with both mechanisms, though often with different shapes.

**Connecting back to the open question about "No MN employment record"**

This three-way comparison offers the most substantive, if still indirect, evidence gathered on this question. The record-absence cluster is dominated by variables plausibly tied to geographic mobility and out-of-state orientation: college-oriented assessments (ACT, SAT), postsecondary exposure, English learner and non-English-home status, and American Indian identity specifically (a population with documented patterns of interstate and reservation-based mobility in this region). This is consistent with a working hypothesis that "no MN record" substantially reflects migration out of the state's tracked labor market, rather than a uniform "labor force exit" story. The genuine-instability cluster (Gender, Economic status, MCA Math/Reading) looks structurally different — tied to access and structural disadvantage rather than mobility — reinforcing that these two clusters likely reflect two different underlying life circumstances, not two measurement artifacts of the same thing.

**Bottom line**

The decision to split `disconnected.cat` into `non_sustained.cat` and `no_record.cat` has now been fully vindicated across all sixteen variables examined in Step 3. What looked like a single, uniform disconnection story in the blended analysis is actually two substantially different stories with different demographic, academic, and geographic correlates — and for most variables, one story clearly dominates. This distinction should be treated as a foundational finding for how the rest of this project's disconnection work gets framed and reported, not a technical footnote.

<br>

## Full Synthesis: Workforce Disconnection Among Non-College Graduates in Southeast Minnesota

**Purpose and Approach**

This analysis examined workforce participation trajectories among Southeast Minnesota high school graduates who did not complete a postsecondary credential (N = 32,878), tracked across the first five years after exiting formal education. Unlike the earlier DV1–DV5 project, which modeled single time-point outcomes for the full cohort and completers, this analysis is trajectory-based and confirmatory/descriptive rather than multivariate — built around a persistence measure (0, 1–2, 3, or 4–5 years disconnected) and examined through cross-tabulations (Cramér's V) and ANOVA (η²) rather than logistic regression.

**Step 1–2: The Descriptive Foundation**

Persistent disconnection is close to the modal outcome for this population: 46.5% of non-completers are Persistently disconnected (4–5 of 5 years), far exceeding Consistently attached (16.2%). Year-by-year tracking revealed a sorting dynamic — unstable employment situations resolve over time into one of two stable poles: Sustained WF–Southeast (growing from 24.9% to 30.5% across Years 1–5) or No MN employment record (growing from 25.9% to 30.6%), which converge to nearly identical size by Year 5.

The critical methodological decision of this analysis was splitting the blended disconnection measure into two independent constructs: **non_sustained.cat** (persistence of unstable employment) and **no_record.cat** (persistence of no MN employment record). Neither component's "Persistent" rate alone (13.1% and 21.1%, respectively) explained the blended 46.5% figure, and a driver breakdown of the persistently-disconnected subgroup confirmed why: No-record driven (45.3%) was the largest single driver, exceeding both Non-sustained driven (28.1%) and Mixed/switching between the two (26.6%). Persistent disconnection in this population is most often a single, consistent problem — and more often a record-absence problem than an employment-instability one.

**Step 3: The Central Finding — Two Distinct, Separable Mechanisms**

Running all sixteen individual-characteristic variables against all three outcome specifications (blended, non-sustained-only, no-record-only) produced the defining result of this entire analysis: disconnection in this population is not one phenomenon with many correlates, but at least two distinct phenomena with substantially different correlates. Most variables sort clearly into one of two clusters:

*The record-absence cluster (the larger group):* attended.ps, took.ACT, ACTCompositeScore.filled, cte.achievement, total.cte.courses.taken, sat.taken, English learner status, Non-English home status, American Indian identity specifically, and edr all showed their blended-table relationships driven substantially or almost entirely by no-record status, not employment instability. In several cases (ACTCompositeScore, sat.taken, edr), the non-sustained relationship dropped to complete non-significance while the no-record relationship remained strong or even strengthened.

*The genuine-instability cluster (smaller but clear):* Gender, Economic status, and MCA Math/Reading scores related specifically to employment instability, largely independent of record-presence. Gender is the cleanest example in the whole project — its Cramér's V *strengthened* for non-sustained employment (0.074 → 0.091) while *collapsing* to near-zero for no-record status (0.016, barely significant).

*A genuinely mixed group:* SpecialEdStatus, Black identity (distinct from American Indian), MCA Science, and PSEO participation showed real relationships with both mechanisms, often in different shapes rather than a single consistent story.

*A null result, resolved only by running all three tables:* avg.unemp.rate and avg.wages.pct.state were weakly significant in the blended measure but null in both mechanism-specific tables — their original significance was very likely a large-sample artifact, not a real, attributable relationship with either pathway.

**Headline Findings**

1.  **Attended.ps (postsecondary attendance without completion) is the single strongest predictor of disconnection found anywhere in this analysis** (blended V = 0.182, the strongest relationship in the entire Step 3 stage), and roughly two-thirds of that strength runs through record-presence rather than employment stability. Even brief postsecondary exposure is strongly associated with staying visible in Minnesota's employment system.

2.  **CTE engagement (both achievement level and course count) is the second-strongest predictor**, and its effect is similarly majority-driven by record-absence. This parallels CTE's role throughout the entire DV1–DV5 and prior non-completer regression work as one of the most durable positive predictors of workforce attachment.

3.  **Standardized test performance splits cleanly by which specific test.** ACT composite score and SAT-taking are both almost purely record-absence markers; MCA Math and Reading are almost purely employment-instability markers; MCA Science is the sole academic variable meaningfully tied to both. This is a genuinely new and specific finding — not simply "academic achievement matters," but a clean mechanism-level split between test types.

4.  **Race/ethnicity shows the largest raw disparities in the entire analysis, and the mechanism differs by group.** American Indian graduates' disparity (66.0% persistently disconnected vs. 44.8% for White graduates in the blended measure) is disproportionately about record-absence (roughly two-thirds of the gap). Black graduates' disparity (62.8% blended) splits more evenly between the two mechanisms. This directly parallels the persistent, unexplained Black-White (and here, especially American Indian) gap that ran through the DV1, DV2, and DV5 multivariate work on completers — now confirmed at the bivariate level in a population that never completed any postsecondary credential, meaning this disparity is not specific to the postsecondary pathway.

5.  **Gender and Economic status are the clearest examples of "genuine instability" variables**, with effects that hold steady or strengthen once no-record status is removed from the outcome, and nearly vanish once non-sustained employment is removed instead.

**Connecting Back to the Open Question**

Earlier in this analysis, what "No MN employment record" actually represents was flagged as an unresolved ambiguity — whether it reflects leaving the state, exiting the labor force, informal work, or some mix. This full bivariate stage doesn't resolve that question definitively, but it does provide the clearest pattern-based evidence gathered anywhere in this project: the record-absence cluster is dominated by variables plausibly tied to geographic mobility and out-of-state orientation — college-oriented assessments (ACT, SAT), postsecondary exposure, English learner and non-English-home status, and American Indian identity specifically. The genuine-instability cluster (Gender, Economic status, MCA Math/Reading) looks structurally different, tied to access and structural disadvantage rather than mobility. This is consistent with a working hypothesis that "no MN record" substantially reflects migration out of Minnesota's tracked labor market for a meaningful share of this population, rather than a single, uniform "labor force exit" story — but it remains a hypothesis supported by pattern, not a confirmed fact.

**Connecting Back to the Full Body of Work**

This analysis reinforces two of the most important findings from the entire project to date. First, the outsized importance of any postsecondary exposure — echoing `attended.ps` and `ps.grad` throughout the DV1–DV5 and non-completer regression models — shows up again here as the single strongest bivariate predictor in a completely different analytic framework. Second, the persistent, unexplained racial disparity — especially for American Indian and Black graduates — appears regardless of population (completers or non-completers), regardless of outcome (employment attachment, credential completion, or disconnection persistence), and regardless of analytic method (multivariate logistic regression, trajectory-based persistence measures, or simple bivariate cross-tabulation). This is the closest thing to a fully triangulated finding in the whole body of work.

**Bottom Line**

The single most important methodological decision in this analysis — separating disconnection into non-sustained employment and no-record status — was fully vindicated. What appeared to be one disconnection story in the blended measure is genuinely two distinct stories with different correlates, different demographic patterns, and (plausibly) different underlying life circumstances. Postsecondary exposure and CTE engagement remain the strongest positive levers identified anywhere in this project, disproportionately operating through record-presence. The Black-White and American Indian-White disparities remain the most robust and troubling unresolved findings across this entire body of work, present in every population, outcome, and method examined so far — and this analysis adds the further nuance that these disparities may run through different mechanisms for different groups, a distinction worth carrying into any policy-facing summary of this work.
